question: A man and a child sing Happy Birthday together, an octave apart. Why does it sound like one tune, not two?
answer: Because every harmonic of the higher note is already in the lower one, so the pair fuses. Whether that makes them the same note is partly learned: Jacoby's team had Tsimane' villagers in Bolivia sing back high tones, and they did not land an octave down on the same note, as Western singers did.
move: Two things that blend perfectly are not, for that reason, the same.
ask: Which things do I treat as identical only because they fit together?

scene.hint: C alone. Tap the next C up, then try other keys with the low C.

moments.name: Octave
moments.text: 1 : 2. Every harmonic of the top C is already in the low one: they fuse.

moments.name: Fifth
moments.text: 2 : 3. Only every other harmonic of G lands on one of C's: blended, but two.

moments.name: One key short
moments.text: 8 : 15. One key below the octave, almost nothing shared, and it grates.

moments.name: Add the octave
moments.text: 2 : 3 : 4. The top C brings nothing new: only more of the low C.

reference: Jacoby, Undurraga, McPherson, Valdés, Ossandón & McDermott, Universal and non-universal features of musical pitch perception revealed by singing, Current Biology 29, 3229-3243, 2019, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2019.08.020
